> **What this case shows** — a surface-EMG signal is a fast, noisy oscillation, but what
> a movement scientist wants is its slowly-varying **amplitude** — the muscle-activation
> **envelope** that says *when* and *how hard* a muscle fires. The classic way to extract
> it is the **Hilbert transform**: form the analytic signal (the EMG plus *i* times its
> Hilbert transform) and take its magnitude. On a real 32-channel forearm-EMG gesture,
> that envelope shows clear **burst activity** — a peak/mean modulation of **6.5**, the
> moment the gesture fires — and identifies the most active channel (14). Because the
> analytic signal is an *exactly-defined* FFT operation, the ecosystem's
> `emgEnvelope(method="hilbert")` reproduces the canonical **`scipy.signal.hilbert`** to
> **machine precision**: the envelopes agree to a maximum absolute difference of
> **6×10⁻¹⁶** across all 32 channels.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to get muscle activation: `emgEnvelope(pe, method="hilbert")` → read the
per-channel envelope → threshold it for onset timing, or feed it to synergy extraction.
**Way of thinking** — the envelope is the *amplitude* of the EMG, not the EMG itself. The
Hilbert method gives it exactly (analytic-signal magnitude); RMS and low-pass are smoothing
alternatives that trade time resolution for smoothness — know which you are using.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioEMG::emgEnvelope()` (hilbert / rms / lowpass), which feeds
`muscleSynergy()`, onset detection, and co-contraction analysis.
:::

## Proposition

On a real 32-channel forearm-EMG gesture (GRABMyo), `emgEnvelope(method="hilbert")`
recovers the muscle-activation envelope (peak/mean modulation 6.5, most active channel
14) and reproduces `scipy.signal.hilbert` to machine precision (max |diff| = 5.6×10⁻¹⁶).

## Question & goal

**The question is whether the ecosystem's muscle-activation envelope is the field-standard
one.** The envelope is the input to onset detection, synergy extraction, and
co-contraction indices — so it must be computed correctly. The goal is a channel-by-channel
head-to-head against `scipy.signal.hilbert`, using the Hilbert method because the analytic
signal is exactly defined and should match to the bit.

## Challenge & approach

The Hilbert envelope is the magnitude of the analytic signal, which is a fixed FFT
operation — zero the negative frequencies, double the positives, inverse-transform, take
the modulus. We compute it with `emgEnvelope(method="hilbert")` and with
`scipy.signal.hilbert`, per channel, and compare.

```
raw EMG (32 ch) → emgEnvelope(method = "hilbert") → activation envelope
                                                    (== |scipy.signal.hilbert|, per channel)
```

## Data

**GRABMyo — forearm & wrist surface-EMG (PhysioNet)**: session1, participant1, gesture10,
trial1 — **32 channels** of forearm EMG, 10240 samples at 2048 Hz. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Conclusion

The muscle-activation envelope the ecosystem reports is exactly the field-standard
`scipy.signal.hilbert` computation — so every downstream analysis built on it (onset
timing, synergies, co-contraction) stands on a validated foundation. The transferable
takeaway: **extract muscle activation with the Hilbert envelope — an exactly-defined
operation you can validate to the bit against the canonical tool — and reserve RMS /
low-pass for when you deliberately want extra smoothing.**

## Open questions

- The envelope is the entry point to activation analysis: an **onset-detection threshold**
  gives muscle-activation timing, the per-channel envelopes feed **muscle-synergy**
  extraction (see the [emg-synergy case](../emg-synergy-grabmyo/)), and comparing the
  Hilbert, RMS, and low-pass envelopes would quantify how the smoothing choice affects
  onset estimates. Extending to activation-timing across a gesture set, or a
  **co-contraction index** between antagonists, would turn a validated estimator into a
  motor-control study. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| amplitude envelope (hilbert / rms / lowpass) | `emgEnvelope()` | PhysioEMG |
| muscle synergies from the envelopes | `muscleSynergy()` | PhysioEMG |
| coordination network | `coordinationNetwork()` | PhysioEMG |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **method** — `"hilbert"` gives the exact analytic-signal envelope (best time resolution);
  `"rms"` (a moving-window RMS) and `"lowpass"` (rectify + low-pass) trade time resolution
  for smoothness. Use Hilbert when you need faithful timing.
- **pre-processing** — band-pass the raw EMG (e.g. 20–450 Hz) before enveloping to remove
  motion artefact and baseline; the envelope inherits whatever you feed it.
- **onset detection** — threshold the envelope (e.g. mean + k·SD of a rest baseline) for
  activation timing.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioEMG)

env <- emgEnvelope(pe, method = "hilbert")          # adds an "envelope" assay
E <- assay(env, "envelope")                          # per-channel activation envelope
apply(E, 2, function(e) max(e) / mean(e))            # burst modulation per channel

# exact by construction: matches |scipy.signal.hilbert(x)| per channel to machine precision
```
